notes:
I've written notes for vv. 1–8, 18–20 and 24–28. vv. 21–23 and most of vv. 9–17 have no notes, and I found nothing from Catholic, Orthodox or Lutheran sources, or about prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. I ran out of search and page reads before I could cover these. The rest of the Enduring Word page and the Matthew Henry page on blueletterbible.org didn't load in full, so they are the best next places to look for vv. 9–23.

---

## 1. The traditional reading

**v. 1:** Guzik says "yet hear now" shows that the judgment warned of at the end of ch. 43 doesn't cancel God's promise. Israel could still know his goodness if they turned back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

**v. 2:** Guzik says "who made you" means God is still at work in his creation, so each person owes something to their Maker. He takes "Jeshurun" to mean "the upright one," a contrast with the name "Jacob." Quoting Bultema, he notes the name shows grace, because God calls a deeply sinful people his "upright one." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/
- Matthew Henry (Concise) also reads Jeshurun as "the upright one." He says God helps those who serve him through their difficulties. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-3.htm

**v. 3:**
- **Water means the Spirit.** Ellicott says the second half of the verse explains the first: the water is the picture and the Spirit is the reality. He hears an echo of Joel 2:28. Barnes agrees that the parallel lines show the water is the Holy Spirit. He prefers the reading "on the thirsty *land*," a picture taken from a desert. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-3.htm
- **What "blessing" covers.** Poole and Benson think the promise was meant to lift the Jews' hearts from worldly things to spiritual ones, and so prepare them for the gospel. Poole includes both spiritual and earthly blessings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-3.htm
- **Who receives it.** The Pulpit Commentary notes that the water is poured only on the one who is thirsty for it. It takes "seed" to include the spiritual Israel, the "Israel of God" of Galatians 6:16. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/44-3.htm
- **Abundance.** Guzik says the word "pour" shows freedom, flow and abundance. He applies it to believers: God pours on whoever is thirsty, asks and receives in faith. He quotes Spurgeon calling for "a fresh baptism into the Holy Ghost." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

**v. 4:** Guzik says the result of the poured-out Spirit is life springing up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/
- A homily in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says that, as a riverside willow shoots up quickly, the person the Spirit is poured on thrives in the life of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/44-3.html

**v. 5:**
- **A sign of belonging.** Guzik says the Spirit marks people as belonging to the Lord and links this to the Spirit's "seal" in Ephesians 1:13. He quotes Spurgeon: the line may mean "subscribe with the hand," recalling servants marked on the hand with their master's name. Spurgeon compares Paul's "marks of the Lord Jesus." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/
- **Gentiles.** Coffman calls the verse "a foretaste of Gentile conversion." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-44.html
- **Spiritual awakening.** The Homiletical Commentary sees it as a general awakening, when people start to take religion seriously. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-44.html

**v. 6:** Guzik argues that an idol can't be "first," since someone has to make it, or "last," since it wears out. Quoting Motyer, he says God is first because his being comes from no one else, and last because he stays supreme at the end. Jesus takes the same title in Revelation 1:17 and 22:13, and Guzik argues that this shows Jesus is the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

**v. 7:** Guzik says only a God outside time can announce things before they happen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/
- Matthew Henry takes "who, as I, shall call" as calling Cyrus to Babylon, announced more than 200 years ahead. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_044.cfm

**v. 8:** Guzik says truly knowing who God is removes fear. He argues that because there is no God besides the LORD, Father, Son and Spirit are each the one LORD. He calls "no other Rock" the only solid ground to build a life on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

**vv. 9–17:** Guzik quotes Adam Clarke, who thought this passage beats anything ever written against idolatry. The craftsmen are "mere men" who get hungry and tired. Half the tree becomes a god and the other half becomes a cooking fire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

**v. 18:** Guzik asks whether God is unjust to "shut their eyes." He says no: people first loved darkness and God then gave them what they wanted, as with Pharaoh's hardened heart and Romans 1. He quotes Motyer: the idolater "chose a delusion and became deluded." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

**v. 20:** Guzik says worshipping an idol is as satisfying as eating ashes. He quotes Motyer: the man holds the idol in his hand, but really the idol holds him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

**v. 24:** Utley explains "Redeemer" as *go'el*: a ransomer who is also a near relative. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20919

**v. 26:** Keil & Delitzsch say that in v. 26 the general titles of God turn into specific prophecies. They take "his servant" as the prophet himself rather than Isaiah naming himself directly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-28.htm

**v. 27:**
- **The Euphrates.** Matthew Henry says this came true when Cyrus took Babylon by draining the Euphrates. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_044.cfm
- **Red Sea and Herodotus.** Keil & Delitzsch hear an echo of the Red Sea crossing but apply the verse to the Euphrates being lowered, citing Herodotus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-28.htm
- **Two readings.** Utley gives the Euphrates reading. He also gives one where God controls water as the true God of fertility, not Baal. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20919

**v. 28:**
- **Proof of foreknowledge.** Poole and Benson say God names Cyrus about 200 years before his birth as undeniable proof that he knows the future, which settles the contest with the idols. Barnes says "shepherd" means ruler and leader. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-28.htm
- **Shepherd title.** Constable notes that "My shepherd" was used of David's kings. Using it of a pagan king shows God would use pagans, since David's line had proved unreliable. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/44-28.html
- **Not a convert.** Utley says the title doesn't mean Cyrus became a believer. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20919
- **Pointing to Christ.** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown call the shepherd a "type of Messiah." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-28.htm
- **Josephus.** Guzik cites Josephus's story that Cyrus read his own name in Isaiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 3, when the promise comes true:**
- **Pentecost.** Coffman sees a glimpse of the new covenant fulfilled above all at Pentecost (Acts 2). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-44.html
- **Not fulfilled at Pentecost.** J. Vernon McGee, a dispensationalist, links it to Joel 2:28–32 but argues that Joel's prophecy was not fulfilled at Pentecost. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/44-3.html
- **Wider than salvation.** Calvin (Reformed) says the verse covers more than the Spirit who gives new birth. It also points to God's grace spread over all creatures. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/44-3.html

**v. 3, "your descendants" and believers' children:**
- **A covenant promise.** One Biblical Illustrator sermon treats it as "God's covenant with Christian parents," alongside Acts 2:39. It says that when God becomes our God, he becomes our children's God. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/44-3.htm
- **Not automatic.** Others in the same sermon collection warn that "religion is not hereditary." https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/44-3.htm Another homily says the promise gives no security without personally accepting Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/44-3.html
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel)** stresses experience: thirsty believers should ask and receive in faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/

I didn't check which denominations these sermon writers belonged to, so treat these as differences of emphasis.

## 3. Other views

**v. 28, modern scholarship:**
- **Second Isaiah.** Guzik notes that many modern scholars see this passage as the strongest argument for a later "Deutero-Isaiah." He argues the name can't simply have been added later, because the whole section is built up to reveal it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-44/
- **Doubts about Josephus.** One older commentary on the Bible Hub page, from the Ellicott/Cambridge group, rejects Josephus's story. It says the story only arose because people assumed Isaiah wrote the words long before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/44-28.htm
- **Cyrus's motives.** The Pulpit Homiletics notes that modern discoveries suggest Cyrus acted out of state policy, and cast doubt on the idea that he believed in one God. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/44-28.htm

**v. 28, the Latin Bible:** Clarke notes the Vulgate reads "Pastor meus es" ("You are my shepherd"). He thinks a Hebrew word dropped out of the text. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/44-28.html
